newsitem.title: FRANCE: German official rebukes France's Seguin on EU.
newsitem.headline: German official rebukes France's Seguin on EU.

text.p: A senior German official on Friday slammed a call by the speaker of the French National Assembly for the European Union to soften economic criteria for joining a single currency, saying the effects would be "catastrophic".

Karl Lamers, foreign policy spokesman for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, rejected suggestions by speaker Philippe Seguin that the EU could find policies better adapted to renewing growth and jobs.
"No, Monsieur Seguin, there is no alternative policy," he wrote in a front-page article in the influential daily Le Monde.

Lamers rejected Seguin's suggestions for the EU to soften strict criteria for nations to qualify for a planned single currency from 1999 and for re-negotiation of the Maastricht Treaty on European Union.
"If the proposal by Philippe Seguin...were adopted by the French government, something which is fortunately very unlikely, the consequences would certainly be catastrophic," he wrote.
Lamers said policies in force in France were a pre-condition for economic growth and job creation and helped keep interest rates low.

Lamers rejected suggestions that rules for a single currency, such as budget rigour, were part of a German diktat, saying: "It's the diktat of supranational reality, of global competition. This reality offers us no other solution."
Seguin, a member of President Jacques Chirac's Rally for the Republic party, was a leader of the narrowly-defeated "No" campaign in a 1992 French referendum on the Maastricht Treaty.
